outline.chapter_title: 1. Introduction to Mathematical Reasoning with LLMs
outline.description: Sets the stage for the textbook by explaining why mathematical reasoning is a challenging yet critically important capability for large language models, summarizing the state‑of‑the‑art, and outlining the goals and contributions of the DeepSeekMath project.
subtopics: Historical context: LLMs and quantitative versus qualitative reasoning
Commercial benchmarks: MATH, GSM8K, SAT, etc.
Gap analysis: Open‑source performance vs closed‑source models (GPT‑4, Gemini-Ultra)
Research objectives of DeepSeekMath
Overview of key innovations: massive math corpus, Group Relative Policy Optimization

outline.description: Reviews core concepts in LLM pre‑training, explaining why code‑centric and mathematics‑centric pre‑training differ, and how data selection shapes downstream reasoning.
subtopics: LLM architecture basics (transformers, tokenization, scaling)
Code training as a proxy for logic and formalism
Mathematical language: symbols, notation, multilingual considerations
Pre‑training objectives: causal LM vs other tasks
Challenges of contamination and de‑contamination in benchmarks

outline.description: Details the iterative pipeline for harvesting high‑quality math content from Common Crawl, emphasizing the design of the fastText seed classifier, data hygiene, multilingual support, and contamination filtering.
subtopics: Seed corpus selection: OpenWebMath and positive/negative examples
fastText classifier training and hyper‑parameter choices
Web page deduplication and near‑deduplication
Iterative retrieval cycles and domain‑level enrichment
Scoring and ranking of candidate pages
Token‑budget evaluation and retention thresholds (40B, 80B, 120B, 160B)
De‑contamination strategies for benchmark overlap
Quantifying corpus size vs. prior corpora (MathPile, Proof‑Pile‑2)
Multilingual analysis: English vs. Chinese coverage

outline.description: Explains how the authors proved the DeepSeekMath corpus was both larger and higher‑quality than existing datasets, using controlled pre‑training experiments and downstream benchmark results.
subtopics: Experimental setup: 1.3B parameter seeds, training budgets
Comparison corpora: 8.9B MathPile, 13.6B OpenWebMath, 38.3B Proof‑Pile‑2
Metrics: Accuracy on 8 math benchmarks with chain‑of‑thought prompting
Learning curves and plateau analysis
Multilingual impact: Chinese benchmarks
Statistical significance tests and ablation insights

outline.description: Covers the configuration, data mix, and training specifics for the base model, establishing its role as a strong mathematical foundation.
subtopics: Initialization from DeepSeek‑Coder‑Base‑v1.5 7B
Data distribution breakdown (56% math corpus, 4% AlgebraicStack, 10% arXiv, 20% GitHub code, 10% NC data)
Learning‑rate schedule and batch sizing
Evaluation methodology: 8 benchmarks in English and Chinese
Results: GSM8K, MATH, CMATH, MMLU‑STEM, Gaokao benchmarks
Tool‑integrated vs. pure reasoning performance
Impact on general reasoning and coding benchmarks (MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP)

outline.description: Describes the curated instruction set, the methodology for annotating solutions with chain‑of‑thought, program‑of‑thought, and tool‑integrated templates, and how these guided the supervised fine‑tuning to produce DeepSeekMath‑Instruct.
subtopics: Dataset construction: 776K examples, English & Chinese coverage
Example types: GSM8K, MATH, MathInstruct, Lila‑OOD, Chinese K‑12 problems
Prompt–completion formats: CoT, PoT, Tool‑integrated
Training protocol: 500 steps, batch size 256, LR 5e‑5
Evaluation protocols: zero‑shot vs few‑shot, tool‑use disabled vs enabled
Benchmark ladder: GSM8K, MATH, SAT, OCW, MMLU‑STEM, Gaokao-MathQA and MATLAB
Closed‑source comparison matrix: GPT‑4, Gemini–Ultra, Inflection‑2, Baichuan‑3, GLM‑4, etc.

outline.description: Introduces reinforcement learning as a post‑SFT stage, contrasts conceptually with prior works (PPO, RFT, DPO), and presents in depth the Group Relative Policy Optimization algorithm.
subtopics: Why RL boosts reasoning: reward‑guided alignment, correcting mistake distribution
PPO recap: actor‑critic, advantage estimation, KL penalty
Limitations of PPO for LLMs: memory cost, token‑wise reward sparsity
GRPO fundamentals: group sampling, baseline from group average, KL regularization
Outcome versus process supervision: reward placement
Iterative GRPO workflow: replay, reference model updates
Algorithmic complexity and resource comparison vs. PPO

outline.description: Examines the design, training, and evaluation of reward models, and how their outputs drive policy updates in GRPO and related RL strategies.
subtopics: Rule‑based reward vs Model‑based reward
Training data for rewards: pairwise comparisons, correctness labels
Generalization to unseen questions
Uncertainty estimation and confidence weighting
Process‑reward models: step‑level signals with Sledgehammer
Reward saturation and clipping effects

outline.description: Provides a consolidated view of all quantitative findings, illustrating how different training stages and data choices influence performance across all evaluation dimensions.
subtopics: Base vs. Instruct vs. RL improvements per benchmark
Self‑consistency gains on MATH
Tool‑use efficacy (program‑of‑thought, TORA)
Multilingual robustness: Chinese datasets
Code‑training impact: two‑stage vs one‑stage
ArXiv ineffectiveness study
Kernels of reinforcement learning: online vs offline, iterative batches
Pass@K vs Maj@K: analysis of RL benefits

outline.chapter_title: 10. Unified Paradigm for Sequential Training Methods
outline.description: Presents a formal framework that captures SFT, RFT, DPO, PPO, and GRPO under a single gradient‑coefficient abstraction, enabling comparison and insight generation.
subtopics: Component triplet: Data Source, Reward, Algorithm
Gradient coefficient formalism
Offline vs Online data sampling: pros/cons
Online vs Offline RL: empirical findings
Process vs Outcome supervision: fine‑grained rewards
Iterative RL and replay buffers
Lessons from rule‑ vs model‑based rewards

outline.chapter_title: 11. Limitations, Ethical Considerations, and Open Questions
outline.description: Contextualises the model’s deficiencies, highlights data and training biases, and discusses potential research directions to close existing gaps.
subtopics: Geometry and theorem‑proof weaknesses
Benchmark contamination subtlety
Scale constraints: few‑shot performance, massive‑parameter gaps
Data bias in source selection (English dominance)
Amplification of misalignment through RL
Human‑in‑the‑loop safety and auditing
Future open‑source trajectories

outline.description: Speculates and recommends concrete research tracks on data, algorithms, and reward design that could push the next generation of open‑source mathematical models beyond current limits.
subtopics: Advanced sampling strategies: tree‑search, speculative decoding
Neural reward models with uncertainty quantification
Weak‑to‑Strong alignment frameworks
Scalable reinforcement methods without critic networks
Cross‑lingual expansion and translation verification
Formal verification pipelines: proof assistants and scaffold generation
Community data infrastructures: shared math corpora and benchmarks
